cards.b:
Not all ancient Indian states were monarchies. Buddhist and Jain texts describe gana-sanghas: states ruled by a council of heads of clans.

  • Examples include the Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy, led by the Licchavis of Vaishali, and the Shakyas of Kapilavastu, the Buddha's own clan.
  • Decisions were made in an assembly hall (santhagara) after debate. Sometimes a vote was taken with wooden tokens called shalakas.
  • In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha lists seven conditions for the Vajjis' welfare. The first is to meet often and in full assembly, and to meet and act in harmony.

Scholars like Romila Thapar warn against calling them democracies in the modern sense. Power lay with an elite of kshatriya clans, not all people. Still, they show that government by discussion has deep roots in India.

cards.h: Economy and welfare in the Arthashastra
cards.b:
The Arthashastra imagines an active, almost interventionist state.

  • The state runs mines, forests, weaving, liquor and salt, and sets up state farms (sita land).
  • Superintendents fix weights and measures, control prices and check traders' profits.
  • The king must support orphans, the old, the sick and helpless women.
  • Labour contracts and wages are regulated. Masters who mistreat workers are fined.
  • Settling new land (janapada nivesha) and building irrigation are royal duties.

This is why some scholars call Kautilya's state a kind of early welfare state. Others warn that its aim was revenue and power, with welfare as a means to keep people productive and loyal.

cards.b:
Sir Syed's work grew into the Aligarh movement, a broad effort to modernise Muslim society.

  • The Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886) spread modern schools across India.
  • He wrote a commentary on the Quran using reason, and urged Muslims to read it afresh rather than rely only on traditional scholars.
  • He supported the English language as the key to jobs and knowledge.
  • He opposed purdah and polygamy in principle, though he moved slowly on women's education.

Aligarh trained a new Muslim middle class. Many of its graduates later led the Muslim League (1906). Others, like the Ali brothers, joined the Khilafat and national movements.

His critics among the ulema of Deoband (founded 1866) rejected his Western leanings.

cards.b:
Gandhi tested his ideas in real campaigns:

  • Champaran (1917): indigo farmers in Bihar against forced cultivation. His first satyagraha in India.
  • Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918): peasants' revenue relief and a mill workers' strike.
  • Non-Cooperation (1920–22): boycott of courts, schools and foreign cloth. He called it off after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922.
  • Civil Disobedience (1930–34): began with the Dandi March against the salt law.
  • Quit India (1942): "Do or die."

Note the pattern. Gandhi chose symbolic issues, like salt, that every Indian could join. He also kept tight control, and withdrew when violence broke out. Critics saw this as caution; he saw it as fidelity to ahimsa.

• Mahad Satyagraha (1927): Dalits drew water from the Chavdar tank, which a public resolution had opened to all.
  • Kalaram Temple entry movement at Nashik (1930–35).
  • Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), with the motto "educate, agitate, organise".
  • Papers: Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Bharat (1927).

On the Constitution, he said India is a "Union of States": the federation is not the result of an agreement, so no state can secede.

He also warned that a constitution is only as good as those who work it. A good one, badly run, will fail.

cards.b:
Roy was a sharp critic of Gandhi. He said Gandhism was a revivalist, backward-looking ideology. It used religion to mobilise peasants while protecting landlords and the Indian bourgeoisie.

He was also critical of nationalism itself. Nationalism, he said, puts the nation above the individual and can easily slide into fascism. This was why he backed the Allies against fascism in the war.

In India in Transition (1922), one of the first Marxist analyses of Indian society, he argued that Indian capitalists would ally with the British, so freedom would need workers and peasants.

These views explain his isolation, but also his distinct place in the syllabus as the radical humanist perspective on Indian nationalism.
